passage:
Wednesday night
Today a two-line email took me forty minutes. I rewrote it six times and still sent it with Swati ma'am's name spelled wrong.
Then I mixed up the March and April sheets in the reconciliation. She caught it before the client did, thank god, but she looked at me like she was trying to work out what had happened to me.
What happened is I'm a fraud. Three months ago I was the intern who finished early. Now I can't add a column without checking it three times, and I still get it wrong.
So I stayed till 9 redoing everything, then came home and couldn't even remember what I'd redone.
The harder I try, the worse it gets. Maybe I'm just not good at this.
Swati ma'am said, "Let's talk tomorrow, 10 am." I'm dreading it.
Neelam

qa.q: How long did the two-line email take?
qa.a: The two-line email took forty minutes.

qa.q: What does Neelam believe is behind the mistakes?
qa.a: Neelam believes being a fraud and 'not good at this' is the reason, without seeing that exhaustion is making everything slower.

qa.q: What might a helpful 10 am talk with Swati ma'am look like?
qa.a: Neelam could admit how tired everything feels, and Swati ma'am could look at the workload and rest together with Neelam rather than asking for more effort.

qa.q: How might Swati ma'am see the change in Neelam?
qa.a: She has watched an intern who once finished early start making repeated mistakes, so she may be puzzled and concerned rather than angry, which is why she asked to talk.

grounding: Shows simple tasks taking far longer, errors multiplying and a sense of being a fraud, with longer hours only deepening the exhaustion.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Friday
Preeti joined the lab in June and was quick and careful. Over the last three weeks I've seen a change. Simple data entry that used to take her an hour now takes most of the morning. She mislabelled two sample sets this week, which she has never done before. Today I found her staring at the same spreadsheet for twenty minutes.
When I asked if she was okay, she said, "I don't know why I'm even here. I'm a fraud." She has been working late every night.
I told her the mistakes are fixable and she is not a fraud. I have reduced her tasks for next week and asked her to see the student counsellor. I'll check in on Monday.
Damini

qa.q: How many sample sets did Preeti mislabel this week?
qa.a: Two sample sets.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt on finding Preeti staring at the same spreadsheet?
qa.a: Damini was likely concerned and worried, noticing a once quick, careful intern suddenly struggling and working late.

qa.q: Why are Damini's steps better than asking Preeti to try harder?
qa.a: Effort alone won't fix exhaustion; reducing tasks and involving the counsellor gives her room to recover.

qa.q: How might Preeti experience Damini's response?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and less alone, hearing she is not a fraud and that her load is lighter.

grounding: Shows a supervisor's note on a student whose simple tasks take longer and mistakes multiply, feeling like a fraud, and support offered.

passage:
Diary, Thursday
Today I sent the wrong file to my manager. Again. Third time this week. Writing a two-paragraph email took me forty minutes. I read it six times and still spelled the client's name wrong.
I used to be the fast one. Now I feel like a fraud who somehow fooled them in the interview. Everyone else seems to get things done.
So I stayed till ten to catch up. Which made me more tired. Which made tomorrow's mistakes more likely. I can see the loop but I can't get out of it.
Simran called and said I sounded like a ghost. She said I should talk to someone. Maybe the office counsellor. I told her I'd think about it.
Dilnaz

qa.q: How long did Dilnaz take to write a two-paragraph email?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling about the mistakes?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels exhausted and ashamed, like a fraud, and trapped in a loop where effort only makes it worse.

qa.q: What turning point does Simran's suggestion offer?
qa.a: Talking to the office counsellor could help Dilnaz step out of the loop, since working longer isn't fixing it.

qa.q: What might Simran be feeling on the call?
qa.a: Simran sounds worried, hearing her friend sound like a ghost and wanting her to get help.

grounding: Shows a young worker whose simple tasks take much longer and mistakes pile up, feeling like a fraud, as effort deepens exhaustion.

passage: The ceiling fan in the electricity board office at Nohar clicked with every turn. Kamal had been on the same meter-reading register since ten. Six months ago he could finish one in forty minutes. Now it was past noon, and he had just found his third wrong entry, a house number copied onto the wrong line. He pressed his palms into his eyes. Fraud, said a voice in his head. They'll find out you were never good at this. He stayed through lunch to redo the page and made a fresh mistake while redoing it. Mehak, at the next desk, slid a glass of chaas towards him. "You've skipped lunch four days running. Is it only the register, or is it everything?" Kamal opened his mouth to say "only the register", and found he couldn't.

qa.q: What mistake had Kamal just found?
qa.a: His third wrong entry, a house number copied onto the wrong line.

qa.q: What does the voice in Kamal's head suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels like a fraud and ashamed, sure others will discover he was never good at the job.

qa.q: Why won't working through lunch fix Kamal's problem?
qa.a: His mistakes come from exhaustion, and harsh self-criticism plus skipped breaks only deepen it; he needs rest and support.

qa.q: What has Mehak noticed about Kamal?
qa.a: Mehak has noticed him skipping lunch four days running and senses the trouble is bigger than one register.

grounding: Shows a worker whose simple tasks now take far longer and whose errors multiply, with self-criticism deepening the exhaustion.
